nameStory: The 'auricled' in this orchid's name comes from the Latin word 'auricula,' meaning 'little ear,' referring to the small ear-like projections at the base of its lip petal. 'Twayblade' is an old English term meaning 'two leaves' - a perfect description since this little orchid produces just two leaves that sit opposite each other on the stem like a pair of green wings.
description: Auricled Twayblade is a small, delicate terrestrial orchid that's easily overlooked in the forest understory. Growing only 3-8 inches tall, it has two broad, oval leaves positioned opposite each other midway up the stem, with a slender spike of tiny yellowish-green flowers above. This inconspicuous little orchid is one of New England's rarest finds, with only a handful of known locations in the region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two broad, oval leaves positioned directly opposite each other on the stem, about halfway up the plant. The leaves feel thin and somewhat succulent, with prominent parallel veins that catch the light.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers arranged in a loose spike above the leaves. Each flower has a distinctive lip petal with small ear-like projections (auricles) at its base that require close inspection to see clearly.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A single, slender stem rising from the forest floor, typically 3-8 inches tall. The plant appears almost fragile, with the two leaves creating the widest part of the otherwise narrow profile.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green stem that feels slightly fleshy to the touch. The stem continues above the leaves as a thinner flowering stalk that may have a slightly ridged texture.

habitat: Found in cool, moist coniferous and mixed forests, often in areas with rich, acidic soil and partial to deep shade. In New England, look for it in northern Maine's boreal forests, typically associated with spruces, firs, and mossy understories. It favors spots with consistent moisture but good drainage, often on gentle slopes or forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in late spring, appearing fresh and bright green against the dark forest floor. The plant is most noticeable at this time before surrounding vegetation fills in.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in early to mid-summer, with the tiny greenish flowers easily missed unless you're looking closely. The two leaves remain the most obvious identification feature throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and fade as temperatures drop, making the plant harder to spot among the autumn leaf litter. Seed capsules may be present if pollination was successful.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely underground, leaving no visible trace above ground until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: This tiny orchid is so rare in New England that it's been documented in only three locations across the entire region - making it more elusive than finding a needle in a haystack, except the haystack is the entire six-state area!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small twayblade orchids, but the Auricled Twayblade's yellowish-green flowers and the tiny ear-like projections on the lip petal set it apart. Remember: if you can see little 'ears' on the flower lip with a hand lens, you've found the auricled species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'twayblade,' this plant is not related to the Twayblade genus (Platanthera) that some field guides reference. The genus Neottia was recently reorganized, so older guides may list this species under the former genus name Listera, which can cause confusion when cross-referencing sources.
compareHints: Among its twayblade relatives, Auricled Twayblade is distinguished by its yellowish-green flowers with the characteristic ear-like projections on the lip petal. Heartleaf Twayblade has heart-shaped leaves and reddish flowers, while Broad-lipped Twayblade has a much wider, more prominent flower lip without the distinctive auricles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's twayblades, Southern Twayblade is distinguished by its deeply split flower lip and preference for acidic coniferous forests.

Heartleaf Twayblade is the only Neottia species in New England with heart-shaped leaves - its relatives like Southern Twayblade have oval leaves, while Broad-lipped Twayblade has broader, more rounded leaves.
Broad-lipped twayblade is distinguished from its twayblade relatives by its wider flower lip and broader leaves.
